record.paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
record.original_question: The asymptotic upper bound of rho(n)/n is never reached.

evidence.quote: The asymptotic upper bound of rho(n)/n is never reached.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For a finite string (word) $w$ over a finite alphabet, a run (also called a maximal repetition) is a maximal occurrence of a periodic factor of exponent at least $2$, i.e., a substring $w[i..j]$ with smallest period $p \le (j-i+1)/2$ that cannot be extended to the left or to the right while preserving the period $p$. Let $\rho(n)$ denote the maximum, taken over all strings of length $n$ over any alphabet, of the number of runs occurring in the string. It is known that the limit superior
$$ \alpha := \limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{\rho(n)}{n} $$
exists and is finite (in fact $\rho(n)<n$ for all $n\ge 1$). Prove or disprove the following: for every positive integer $n$,
$$ \frac{\rho(n)}{n} < \alpha. $$
That is, the asymptotic upper bound of $\rho(n)/n$ is never attained for any finite $n$.
artifact.category_tag: combinatorics on words / runs in strings
artifact.status_search_result: While the classical "runs" conjecture ρ(n) < n was resolved affirmatively by Bannai, I, Inenaga, Nakashima, Takeda, and Tsuruta (SIAM J. Comput., 2017), the finer statement that ρ(n)/n never attains its asymptotic limsup α does not appear to have been settled in the literature accessible by search. The exact value of α and the precise behaviour of ρ(n)/n for finite n remain subjects of active investigation, so the status of this specific conjecture is unclear.

status_evidence.title: The "Runs" Theorem
status_evidence.snippet: Bannai et al. prove ρ(n) < n using a Lyndon-word based characterization of runs.
status_evidence.claim: The bound ρ(n) < n (a weaker form of the runs conjecture) is proven.

status_evidence.title: The "Runs" Theorem | SIAM Journal on Computing
status_evidence.snippet: Published version of the proof that the maximum number of runs in a string of length n is less than n.
status_evidence.claim: The result ρ(n) < n is established, but the question of whether ρ(n)/n attains its limsup is not addressed there.
